# Introduction

This project investigates writer information in a simulated handwritten-digit dataset using two neural-network approaches. The first approach uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) to directly predict the identity of the writer. The second uses a Siamese neural network to determine whether two handwriting samples were produced by the same person.

The dataset contains 25,000 images of handwritten digits generated by 20 writers. Each writer completed five independent recording sessions and produced 50 examples of each digit from 0 to 4 in each session. The images have dimensions 28 × 28 pixels. The handwriting is simulated and writing style varies both within and between sessions.

The objectives were to investigate visual variation between writers, digits and sessions, build a CNN for writer identification, construct a Siamese network for same-writer verification, justify train, validation and test splits, conduct limited hyperparameter optimisation, and compare the two approaches.

## Limitations of the simulated data

The data are simulated and therefore cleaner and more controlled than handwriting collected in realistic conditions. Only 20 writers and five digits are represented. Real-world handwriting may also contain scanning artefacts, different pens and paper, varying resolution, incomplete strokes and background noise.

# Train, validation and test strategy

## CNN split by session

For the CNN, Sessions 1–3 were used for training, Session 4 was used for validation and Session 5 was used for testing.

**INSERT CODE CHUNK FOR SPLITTING OF CNN**

This split evaluates whether the model can identify a known writer in a new recording session.

## Random-image baseline split

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

split_rand <- sample(
  c("train", "val", "test"),
  nrow(meta),
  replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2)
)

table(split_rand)
prop.table(table(split_rand))
```

The random-image split is included as a baseline. It mixes images from all sessions across train, validation and test subsets, which can result in a more optimistic performance estimate than the session-held-out split.

## Siamese split by writer

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

w <- sample(1:20)

writers <- list(
  train = w[1:14],
  val = w[15:17],
  test = w[18:20])


split_sia <- case_when(
  meta$person_id %in% writers$train ~ "train",
  meta$person_id %in% writers$val ~ "val",
  TRUE ~ "test")


stopifnot(
  length(intersect(writers$train, writers$test)) == 0,
  length(intersect(writers$train, writers$val)) == 0,
  length(intersect(writers$val, writers$test)) == 0)

```

The Siamese split evaluates whether the model can compare handwriting from writers who were not seen during training.

# Siamese network

## Constructing same-writer and different-writer pairs

```{r}
rows <- lapply(
  c(train = "train", val = "val", test = "test"),
  function(s) which(split_sia == s)
)

make_pairs <- function(rows, n, same_digit = TRUE) {

  p <- meta$person_id[rows]
  d <- meta$digit[rows]

  by_pd <- split(rows, paste(p, d))
  by_p <- split(rows, p)
  writers <- unique(p)

  pick <- function(v) v[sample.int(length(v), 1)]

  a <- sample(rows, n, replace = TRUE)
  y <- rep(c(1L, 0L), length.out = n)
  b <- integer(n)

  for (k in seq_len(n)) {
    pa <- meta$person_id[a[k]]
    da <- meta$digit[a[k]]

    if (y[k] == 1L) {
      pool <- if (same_digit) by_pd[[paste(pa, da)]] else by_p[[as.character(pa)]]
      pool <- setdiff(pool, a[k])
    } else {
      pb <- pick(setdiff(writers, pa))
      pool <- if (same_digit) by_pd[[paste(pb, da)]] else by_p[[as.character(pb)]]
    }

    b[k] <- pick(pool)
  }

  tibble(
    a = a,
    b = b,
    y = y,
    digit_a = meta$digit[a],
    digit_b = meta$digit[b],
    sess_a = meta$session[a],
    sess_b = meta$session[b]
  )
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

pairs <- list(
  train = make_pairs(rows$train, 30000),
  val = make_pairs(rows$val, 6000),
  test = make_pairs(rows$test, 6000)
)

table(pairs$train$y)
table(pairs$val$y)
table(pairs$test$y)
```

Pairs were balanced between same-writer and different-writer examples. The same digit was used in both images of each pair so that the network was encouraged to learn writer style rather than digit identity.

## Convert pairs to model inputs

```{r}
get_xy <- function(pr) {
  list(
    x = list(
      x[pr$a, , , , drop = FALSE],
      x[pr$b, , , , drop = FALSE]
    ),
    y = matrix(pr$y, ncol = 1)
  )
}

tr <- get_xy(pairs$train)
va <- get_xy(pairs$val)
te <- get_xy(pairs$test)
```

## Encoder and contrastive loss

```{r}
build_encoder <- function(emb = 32, filters = 32, dropout = 0.2) {
  keras_model_sequential(
    input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)
  ) |>
    layer_conv_2d(filters, 3, activation = "relu", padding = "same") |>
    layer_max_pooling_2d(2) |>
    layer_conv_2d(filters * 2, 3, activation = "relu", padding = "same") |>
    layer_max_pooling_2d(2) |>
    layer_flatten() |>
    layer_dropout(dropout) |>
    layer_dense(emb)
}

contrastive_loss <- function(margin = 1) {
  function(y_true, y_pred) {
    y_true <- op_cast(y_true, "float32")
    pos <- y_true * op_square(y_pred)
    neg <- (1 - y_true) *
      op_square(op_maximum(margin - y_pred, 0))
    op_mean(pos + neg)
  }
}
```

## Siamese model builder

```{r}
build_siamese <- function(
  emb = 32,
  filters = 32,
  dropout = 0.2,
  margin = 1,
  lr = 1e-3
) {

  encoder <- build_encoder(emb, filters, dropout)

  in_a <- keras_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
  in_b <- keras_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))

  encoded_a <- encoder(in_a)
  encoded_b <- encoder(in_b)

  diff <- layer_subtract(list(encoded_a, encoded_b))

  dist <- layer_lambda(
    diff,
    function(d) {
      op_sqrt(
        op_maximum(
          op_sum(op_square(d), axis = -1L, keepdims = TRUE),
          1e-9
        )
      )
    }
  )

  model <- keras_model(
    inputs = list(in_a, in_b),
    outputs = dist
  )

  model |> compile(
    optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = lr),
    loss = contrastive_loss(margin)
  )

  model
}
```

# Siamese hyperparameter tuning

```{r}
library(tidyverse); library(pROC)

run_config <- function(emb, filters, dropout, margin, lr, seed) {
  set_random_seed(seed)
  m <- build_siamese(emb = emb, filters = filters, dropout = dropout,
                     margin = margin, lr = lr)
  h <- m |> fit(tr$x, tr$y, epochs = 20, batch_size = 128,
                validation_data = list(va$x, va$y), verbose = 0,
                callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(
                  monitor = "val_loss", patience = 3, restore_best_weights = TRUE)))
  d <- as.numeric(predict(m, va$x, verbose = 0))
  r <- roc(pairs$val$y, d, levels = c(0, 1), direction = ">", quiet = TRUE)
  fpr <- 1 - r$specificities; fnr <- 1 - r$sensitivities
  list(val_auc = as.numeric(auc(r)),
       val_eer = fpr[which.min(abs(fpr - fnr))],
       epochs  = length(h$metrics$loss),
       history = h)
}

base <- list(emb = 32, filters = 32, dropout = 0.2, margin = 1, lr = 1e-3)

# One setting at a time: each row changes exactly one value
vary <- bind_rows(
  tibble(param = "baseline", value = 0),
  tibble(param = "emb",      value = c(8, 16, 64)),
  tibble(param = "margin",   value = c(0.5, 2)),
  tibble(param = "lr",       value = c(1e-4, 3e-4, 3e-3)),
  tibble(param = "dropout",  value = c(0.5)),
  tibble(param = "filters",  value = c(16, 64))
)

grid <- vary |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(cfg = list(modifyList(base,
            if (param == "baseline") list() else setNames(list(value), param)))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  cross_join(tibble(seed = 1:3))

fits <- map2(grid$cfg, grid$seed, \(cfg, s) do.call(run_config, c(cfg, seed = s)))

res <- grid |> select(param, value, seed) |>
  mutate(val_auc = map_dbl(fits, "val_auc"),
         val_eer = map_dbl(fits, "val_eer"),
         epochs  = map_int(fits, "epochs"))

# Summary: mean and sd over seeds
summ <- res |> group_by(param, value) |>
  summarise(auc_mean = mean(val_auc), auc_sd = sd(val_auc),
            eer_mean = mean(val_eer), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(auc_mean))
summ

# Sensitivity plot: validation AUC per setting, spread over seeds
ggplot(res, aes(factor(value), val_auc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", colour = "red", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~param, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Validation AUC")
```


#The best model
```{r}
best_row <- summ[1, ]                 # highest mean validation AUC
best_cfg <- modifyList(base, setNames(list(best_row$value), best_row$param))
# (if the best row is "baseline", use base as is)

set_random_seed(2026)
best <- do.call(build_siamese, best_cfg)
best |> fit(tr$x, tr$y, epochs = 20, batch_size = 128,
            validation_data = list(va$x, va$y), verbose = 0,
            callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(
              monitor = "val_loss", patience = 3, restore_best_weights = TRUE)))
```

The strongest previously observed setting increased the learning rate to 0.003 while leaving the remaining baseline parameters unchanged. This produced a validation AUC of approximately 0.984.

#Use test model

```{r}
# Select the threshold using validation data
val_dist <- as.numeric(predict(best, va$x, verbose = 0))

val_roc <- roc(
  pairs$val$y, val_dist,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  direction = ">",
  quiet = TRUE
)

threshold <- as.numeric(
  coords(
    val_roc,
    x = "best",
    best.method = "youden",
    ret = "threshold",
    transpose = FALSE
  )[1]
)

# Classify test pairs using the validation threshold
actual <- pairs$test$y
predicted <- as.integer(test_dist <= threshold)

TP <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 1)
TN <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 0)
FP <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 0)
FN <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 1)

sensitivity <- TP / (TP + FN)
specificity <- TN / (TN + FP)

cat("Test AUC:", round(test_auc, 4), "\n")
cat("Test EER:", round(test_eer, 4), "\n")
cat("Test Sensitivity:", round(sensitivity, 4), "\n")
cat("Test Specificity:", round(specificity, 4), "\n")
```

# Comparison of CNN and Siamese approaches

The CNN and Siamese network address related but different problems. The CNN performs closed-set identification: it predicts which of the 20 known writers produced an image. The Siamese network performs writer verification: it determines whether two samples were produced by the same person.

**what was the accuracy of both neural networks**

These values should not be directly compared as if they represent the same prediction problem. The CNN tests known-writer identification in a new session, while the Siamese model tests matching performance on previously unseen writers.

# Digit and session effects

We can also discuss whether cross-session matching is more difficult than same-session matching and relate this to the CNN results.

# Limitations

Several limitations should be considered. The data are simulated and therefore do not represent all difficulties encountered in real handwriting. Only 20 writers and five digits are represented. The CNN evaluates new sessions from known writers rather than completely new writers. Siamese performance depends on the pair-generation procedure. Neural-network training is stochastic, so small numerical differences may occur between executions.
